anchors.text: Fig. 1 Experimental configuration and model of tetrapolar conductivity measurements. a) The tested sample is represented as two isotropic homogeneous layers of infinite lateral dimensions where layer 1 (with conductivity  $ \sigma_1 $) is the articular cartilage of thickness “d,” and layer 2 (with conductivity  $ \sigma_2 $) is the subchondral bone, taken to be of infinite thickness. There are three tetrapolar electrode configurations used in this study where the current is injected using one of three possible pairs of electrodes (#1–#8, #2–#7, #3–#6) while the potential difference is always measured by the central electrode pair (#4–#5). b) A light micrograph shows the 300  $ \mu $m regular spacing of the 8 electrodes of 50  $ \mu $m diameter. The faint circles above the electrodes are the nylon mesh in cross-section.

Fig. 2 Theoretical prediction and calibration of the apparent conductivity as function of the thickness of layer 1. a) The apparent conductivity (Eq. 2) for the three tetrapolar configurations as a function of the thickness of layer 1 (d), calculated using model assumptions explained in Fig. 1 and with $\sigma_1 = 1$ S/m, $\sigma_2 = 0.2$ S/m and $a = 300$ $\mu$m. The model predicts that the apparent conductivity approaches that of layer 1 when layer 1 thickness is $>2\times$ the inter-electrode spacing ($\sim600$ $\mu$m for equidistant configuration #3-#6) and approaches that of layer 2 when the thickness of layer 1 is $\sim10$ $\times$ less than the inter-electrode spacing ($\sim30$ $\mu$m for equidistant configuration #3-#6). Spacing apart the injection electrodes (using #2-#7, #1-#8) results in lower apparent conductivity due to deeper penetration of the current and therefore greater influence of the lower conductivity of layer 2. b) The apparent conductivity was measured using three different NaCl concentrations (0.03 M, 0.1 M, 0.5 M) with electrical conductivities ($\sigma_1$) of (0.34 S/m, 1.04 S/m, 4.54 S/m). The distance, $d$, between the upper post and chamber bottom was varied to change the thickness of the layer of known conductivity, $\sigma_1$, and measured apparent conductivity was normalized as $\sigma_{\text{app}} / \sigma_1$ shown in the figure. The $x$ axis in Figure 2b was shifted such that the point of contact was taken as 50 $\mu$m separation rather than 0 $\mu$m separation, due to non-parallelism of the two surfaces. The mean$\pm$sd of these three normalized conductivities (3 salt concentrations) are shown for each of the tetrapolar configurations (○ for #3-#6, ■ for #2-#7, △ for #1-#8) along with the theoretical prediction calculated using Eq. 3 with $\sigma_2 = 0$.

Fig. 3 Experimental apparatus for electrical conductivity measurement. a) Articular cartilage slices (2 mm wide, 12 mm long and 200-550  $ \mu $m thick) were positioned on the center of the microelectrode array and slightly compressed (5  $ \mu $m) under uniaxial unconfined compression geometry to assure good electrical contact. Electrical conductivity was measured using the equidistant electrode configuration with electrodes #3 and #6 injecting current. b) Electrical conductivity of disk-shaped samples (3.5 mm diameter with full-thickness articular cartilage attached to underlying bone) were measured by gluing the bone surface onto a transparent plastic plate that was then glued to a stainless steel bolt that was heavy enough (7.2 g) to ensure good contact when placing the articular cartilage surface in contact with the exposed electrodes. All three tetrapolar configurations were used to measure conductivity in this case. For both types of experiments, the test chamber was filled with 0.15 M phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) that has an electrical conductivity of 1.52 S/m. An alternating current of 1  $ \mu $A amplitude was injected at frequencies in the range of 10 Hz to 1000 Hz.

Fig. 4 Example raw data. a) Typical measured sinusoidal voltage for the equidistant tetrapolar configuration. b) Fourier-transformed raw data shows the ratio of the measured voltage to applied current, amplitude and phase (voltage-current) and total harmonic distortion (THD) as function of frequency.

Fig. 6 Apparent conductivity as a function of sample thickness for the three tetrapolar configurations (example data). The apparent conductivity of disk samples were obtained with the chamber of Fig. 3b. The cartilage thickness was reduced by removing slices consecutively with a vibratome and the sample thickness (cartilage+bone) was measured with a micrometer after each slice was removed. The apparent conductivity decreases with decreasing cartilage thickness, and when the injecting electrodes are farther apart, as predicted by the model (Fig. 2).

Fig. 7 Histological appearance of cartilage/bone disks with and without cutting to reduce cartilage thickness. Disk samples were matched as adjacent duplicates during isolation where one of each duplicate was used for conductivity measurements as a function of cartilage thickness (Fig. 3b) and then preserved by aldehyde fixation (B, D, F) while the other was chemically fixed directly without cutting (A,C,E). Disks were washed, embedded, sectioned and stained with toluidine blue. The last cut usually arrived just above the tidemark (B), however some uncalcified cartilage could remain (D). Variations in bone porosity and the thickness of the subchondral bone plate were evident (A and E to C). With respect to Table 2, B=sample 2, D=sample 5, F=sample 9. UC=uncalcified cartilage, CC=calcified cartilage. Scale bar =300 μm.

Fig. 8 Comparison of cartilage thickness measured by conductivity and by a micrometer plus histology for 4 example disks. Conductivity measurements were performed on each disk using all three tetrapolar configurations at each thickness. These 3 conductivity values (Type A data) were used as inputs to a fitting routine that minimized differences between the 3 conductivity values and Eq. 2 by fixing  $ \sigma_2 $ to either 0.2 S/m ( $ \odot $) or 0 S/m ( $ \square $) and varying  $ \sigma_1 $ and  $ d $. The resulting best fit thickness $ ^+ $ after each cut are shown compared to the thickness ( $ \triangle $) obtained by subtracting the bone thickness measured microscopically on the histological section from the total disk thickness (cartilage+bone) measured with a micrometer after removing each slice. The thickness values obtained from best fit conductivity measurements using  $ \sigma_2 = 0 $ S/m appeared to match histology/micrometer thickness values better than those obtained using  $ \sigma_2 = 0.2 $ S/m.

anchors.text: Figure 1 Schematic representation of loading regimes of articular cartilage. Dynamic compression of the extracellular matrix induces deformation of cells and matrix, hydrostatic pressure gradients, and interstitial fluid flow. Fluid convection and separation of counterions from the fixed charge groups of the proteoglycan constituents gives rise to electrical streaming potentials and currents. In contrast, tissue shear deformation of a poroelastic tissue does not induce volumetric changes, intratissue fluid flow, or pressure gradients.

Figure 2 (A) Unconfined compression of a cylindrical disk specimen, which has been modeled by an axisymmetric finite-element implementation (89). (B) The relative fluid velocity profile in the upper quadrant of A at the end of a 60-sec-constant-velocity, 25  $ \mu $m ramp compression of a 1-mm-thick disk that is 3 mm in diameter. (C) Current density profile at the end of the ramp compression (see 89 for details). (D) Axial strain profile predicted (89) for a statically compressed disk with depth-dependent equilibrium modulus (e.g. 92).

Figure 3 (A) $ ^{35} $S-Sulfate incorporation as a measure of proteoglycan synthesis in cartilage explants that were removed from culture at 2, 4, 8, 24, or 48 h after simultaneous exposure to 0 or 300 ng/ml of IGF-1 and were held at either 1.0-mm cut thickness or 0.65-mm compressed thickness (reproduced from 75, by permission of the publisher). (B) $ ^{3} $H-Proline radiolabel incorporation as a measure of total protein synthesis in cartilage disks during a 2-h label terminating at 2, 4, 16, 24, and 48 h after treatment with IGF-1 and/or imposition of a 2% sinusoidal strain at 0.1 Hz. Values are normalized to those of control disks [0 ng/ml IGF-1 with no compression (reproduced from 100, by permission of the publisher)].

Figure 4 Sulfate and proline radiolabel incorporation (for proteoglycan and total protein synthesis) in cartilage disks subjected to dynamic tissue shear strain of 1% amplitude at 0.1 Hz, compared with control disks maintained at the same static-offset compressed thickness but with no dynamic shear (reproduced from 101, by permission of the publisher).

Figure 5 Aggrecan and type-II collagen gene expression and biosynthesis in response to a static compression to 50% of cut thickness (reproduced from 92, by permission of the publisher). (A) mRNA levels were quantified and normalized to glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH) as a function of time after step compression. (B) Sulfate and proline radiolabel incorporation for PG and total protein synthesis as a function of time after step compression, normalized to values of free-swelling controls at 24 h (see 104 for details).

Figure 6 (A) Low and (B) high magnification of chondrocyte within a native cartilage tissue disk subjected to 20% axial static unconfined compression, fixed, and visualized by electron microscope. (B) Ordered, anisotropic morphology or rough endoplasmic reticulum during compression, compared with the more istropic, randomly ordered distribution in uncompressed controls (see 111 for details). (C) CHO cells showing green fluorescence protein-6-sulfotransferase fusion protein transfected into cells and localized within rough endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus, visualized by using two-photon fluorescence microscopy.

anchors.text: Fig. 1. Selective labeling of Gdf5-expressing cells in Gdf5 $ ^{CreERT2} $ mice. At birth, Gdf5 $ ^{Cre} $;R26R $ ^{25Green} $ labeled cells are found throughout the joint, including within the articular cartilage (white arrow) and the putative secondary ossification center (yellow arrowhead) (A). After tamoxifen administration to Prg4 $ ^{CreERT2} $/R26R $ ^{tdTomato} $ mice at 1 month of age, labeled cells are found throughout the superficial layer of the articular cartilage (C). One week after injury, cells within the defect site (dotted line) are Prg4+, indicating that cells with a Prg4-expressing lineage participate in the acute injury response (D).

Fig. 8. (A) Scheme of 3D bioprinting process of articular cartilage engineering. Reprinted with permission from Ref. [51]. (B) Chitosan scaffold at scanning electron microscopy (SEM). Reprinted with permission from Ref. [52]. (C) Images of printed scaffolds. Reprinted with permission from Ref. [53].

Fig. 9. (A) Gross morphology of scaffolds. Reprinted with permission from Ref. [54]. (B) Schematic illustration of fabrication process. Reprinted with permission from Ref. [55]. (C) Microscopic analysis of GO. (a) Transmission electron microscopy microphotography of few-layer GO sheets. (b) Lateral size distribution of GO particles. (c) Liquid crystalline properties of an aqueous suspension of GO observed with parallel polarizer/analyzer and (d) crossed polarizer/analyzer filters. The liquid crystal (LC) order is maintained in a wetted flake of GO, which is observed in the (e) parallel polarizer/analyzer and (f) crossed polarizer/analyzer (with a retardation plate) filters. Reprinted with permission from Ref. [56].

Fig. 10. (A) HBC/OCS hydrogel implants with various shapes. Reprinted with permission from Ref. [57]. (B) 3D reconstructions obtained from  $ \mu $CT scan: (a) top, (b) lateral, and (c) prospective views of a selected volume of interest of a printed scaffold with dimensions  $ 6 \times 6 \times 1 \, mm^3 $ and  $ 0^\circ $– $ 90^\circ $ fibers orientation. Reprinted with permission from Ref. [58]. (C) Schematic illustration of 3D printing of scaffolds as well as the isolation and seeding of cells on the printed scaffolds. Reprinted with permission from Ref. [59].

Fig. 11. (A) CAD-based 3D bioprinting process. Reprinted with permission from Ref. [60]. (B) Schematic illustration of electrospinning fiber-reinforced CDM-based 3D-printed scaffold for cartilage regeneration. Reprinted with permission from Ref. [61].

Fig. 14. (A) (a) Outline of experimental groups, whereby 3D printed polymer frames were combined with cells encapsulated in alginate. (b) Representative macroscopic plan view of the hybrid constructs after 3 and 28 days in culture. Reprinted with permission from Ref. [66]. (B) Process of printing the biomimetic meniscal scaffold. The bioink was prepared by mixing ultrasonicated MECM, GelMA, and MFCs at specific concentrations. Meanwhile, the sheep meniscus was scanned by CT, modeled in Mimics, and used to plan the printing path. The prepared bioink and PCL were printed under the designed printing parameters according to the established printing path, and finally, printing of the biomimetic meniscal scaffold was completed. Reprinted with permission from Ref. [67]. (C) (a–c) Histological and immunohistochemical staining of all 3D bioprinted constructs groups after (a) 1, (b) 21, and (c) 42 days of in vitro culture. Scale bar, 500  $ \mu $m. Reprinted with permission from Ref. [68].

Fig. 16. (A) (a) 4D bioprinting stage including a custom-designed adapter for incorporating a cylindrical magnet that forces real-time remodeling of the bioink while bioprinting. (b, c) Bioprinted construct with three layers resembling the structure of native articular cartilage. (d, e) Cross-sectional views of bioprinted constructs for easier visualization of different layers. (B) Immunohistochemical analyses of bioprinted samples. Scale bar, 200  $ \mu $m. (C) Incorporation of printed layers with horizontally aligned collagen fibers to layers with randomly distributed fibers observed by second-harmonic and bright field images. Reprinted with permission from Ref. [148].

Fig. 12. Schematic of 3D bioprinting approach for engineering of articular cartilage. hMSC-laden fibrinogen was used as a bioink for printing in a self-healing supporting bath of PEG-alginate prepolymer mixture, supplemented with thrombin. Thrombin interacted with fibrinogen and polymerized during bioprinting, forming soft fibrin fibers inside the hard PEG-alginate hydrogel and creating a suitable environment for chondrocyte differentiation within a mechanically robust construct. This system allows for the bioengineering of 3D native-like cartilage tissue. Reprinted with permission from Ref. [62].

anchors.text: Fig. 1. Physico-chemical characterisation of SF/PEDOT hydrogels. (A-B) Time-sweep rheological analysis of SF based hydrogels showing changes in (A) storage and loss moduli and (B) complex viscosity over time, showing progressive gelation at 37°C without a crossover point. Insets of (A) show visual changes in viscous nature of SF3/PEDOT over time (in comparison to SF3) and (B) show time sweep gelation profile of SF6/PEDOT. (C) Shear-thinning behaviour of SF/PEDOT hydrogels with increasing SF concentration. (D) FT-IR spectra of SF3 and SF3/PEDOT hydrogels before (BG) and after gelation (AG) and during partial gelation (PG) stage and (E) Secondary structure composition derived from FT-IR amide I peak deconvolution confirming β-sheet induction as gelation progresses. (F-G) Electrical conductivity (F) and functional demonstration of electronic conductivity showing a blue LED illumination via current passed through lyophilised SF/PEDOT sponges (G). (H) Injection force profiles (force vs. extrusion distance) for different SF/PEDOT formulations (SF1 and SF3) before gelation and at partial-gelation stage using 18 G and 20 G needles. (I-J) Quantification of peak injection force (I) and sustained injection force (J), highlighting injectability across needle gauges and stiffness variation between formulations (Data are Mean ± S.D. (n = 3) *p < 0.05, **p < 0.01, ***p < 0.0001). Comparisons not shown with asterisks are not significant. (K-L) Representative syringe injection images (top view) showing structural integrity of SF3/PEDOT (BG and PG states) extruded through 18 G (K) and 20 G (L) needles into 1X PBS. (For interpretation of the references to colour in this figure legend, the reader is referred to the Web version of this article.)

Fig. 2. Tuneable mechanical, rheological and biodegradability of SF/PEDOT hydrogels through variation in SF concentration to optimise structural stability and injectable properties. (A) Stress-strain curves, (B) compressive modulus, (C) Swelling ratio, (D) porosity and (E) biodegradation profile (physiological proteolytic environment at 37°C) of various SF/PEDOT hydrogels. (F) SEM of freeze-dried SF/PEDOT hydrogels showing the microporous architecture. (G) shows representative images of the conductive hydrogels before and after biodegradation study. (H) Strain amplitude sweep showing viscoelastic response and mechanical integrity (G' vs G') under deformation. (I) Frequency sweep confirming viscoelastic stability across a physiological range of frequencies. (J & K) Thixotropic behaviour showing (J) step-strain time sweep (strain recovery) demonstrating dynamic mechanical reversibility and resilience to cyclic deformation and (K) rapid recovery of complex viscosity post-deformation under alternating shear stress. [(B&C) Data are Mean ± S.D. (n = 3); *p < 0.05, **p < 0.001].

Fig. 3. Design, working principle, and optimisation of the non-invasive WES system utilising SF/PEDOT hydrogel as a capacitive receiver. (A) Schematic illustration of the WES system setup. A pulsed oscillating electric field is applied across a dielectric medium (polystyrene + glass or glass only), inducing displacement current that non-invasively couple into the SF/PEDOT hydrogel, generating a secondary electric field leading to ionic/electronic conductivity due to its low charge transfer resistance ( $ R_{ct} $). (B) Representative oscilloscope outputs demonstrating peak to peak voltage ( $ V_{pp} $) generated in SF/PEDOT hydrogel across a copper receiver without media, with media (RPMI), and across ex-vivo porcine tissue. Insets: close up view of each condition. (C) Quantitative comparison of  $ V_{pp} $ across conditions, highlighting the capacitive signal transmission properties of SF/PEDOT hydrogels in biologically relevant environments. (D) Time-domain waveform outputs showing SF/PEDOT's response to varying input voltages (1-4 V) at 10 kHz. Frequency-dependent analysis of output  $ V_{pp} $ (E) at 2 V input across a range from 10 Hz to 1 MHz across glass in presence of RPMI medium and (F) at 4 V input across range from 10 Hz to 10 kHz across porcine muscle tissue. (G) Bode plot of the SF3/PEDOT hydrogel showing its frequency-dependent impedance and phase. (H) Nyquist plot of the SF3/PEDOT hydrogel. Inset: high frequency region and fitting to determine charge transfer resistance. [(C & E) Data are Mean ± SD, n = 3; *p < 0.05, ***p < 0.0001. Comparisons not shown with asterisks are not significant.

Fig. 5. WES enhances Cx43 expression and gap junction formation in hiPSC derived cortical astrocytes (CTX-ASTRO) embedded in SF/PEDOT hydrogel. (A) Schematic depicting the experimental workflow where hiPSC-derived CTX ASTRO were encapsulated in the SF based the hydrogels and subjected to WES as indicated. Representative confocal images showing (B) CTX-ASTRO (cultured at higher density) stained for GFAP (green), Cx43 (red), and DAPI (blue); and (C) CTX-ASTRO (cultured at low density) stained with S100β (cyan), SOX9 (magenta) and DAPI (blue), across groups as labelled. Higher magnification panels [bottom panel of (B)] show increased Cx43 signal and elongated astrocytic morphology in response to SF/PEDOT + WES treatment. (D) High-magnification representative Cx43/DAPI images showing distinct Cx43 puncta (dotted white circles) in the electrically stimulated groups. (E) Quantification of Cx43-positive astrocytes (%), demonstrating significant upregulation in SF3/PEDOT + WES condition. (F) Quantification of Cx43 puncta per cell indicates a higher number of gap junction-like structures in electrically stimulated hydrogel environments. Statistical significance: ***p < 0.001; comparisons not shown with asterisks are not statistically significant. Scale bars: 50 μm (B & C), 20 μm [zoomed panel in (C)], 10 μm [(D)]. (For interpretation of the references to colour in this figure legend, the reader is referred to the Web version of this article.)

Fig. 7. WES delivered via SF/PEDOT hydrogel modulates astrocyte phenotype from pro-inflammatory to pro-regenerative phenotype. ELISA-based cytokine analysis showing the impact of WES on reactive astrocytes in releasing (A) IL-10, (B) TNF- $ \alpha $, (C) IL-6, (D) CXCL10, and (E) GM-CSF by CTX-ASTRO encapsulated in SF based hydrogels under four conditions: control or basal culture (+WES/−Factors) (−WES/−Factors), WES only (+WES), inflammatory challenge using microglial secretion factors only (+Factors), and combined WES and inflammatory challenge (+WES + Factors). Data are Mean ± SD (n = 3 independent cultures) with symbols denote independent biological replicates. Statistics: Kruskal-Wallis with Dunn's post-hoc; p* < 0.05, p** < 0.01; comparisons not shown with asterisks are not statistically significant.

Fig. 4. Charge polarisation induced capacitive-coupling based WES delivered through SF/PEDOT hydrogels modulates macrophage polarisation. (A) Schematic of the experimental workflow: human blood-derived macrophages (hBDMs) were seeded on SF or SF/PEDOT hydrogels, stimulated using non-invasive WES (2V, 10 kHz biphasic pulsed waveform, 1 hour), and analysed after 24 h by immunocytochemistry and ELISA. anchors.text: Figure 1. This image illustrates the electrical properties of natural bone and cartilage and the role of electroactive biomaterials in osteochondral regeneration. Piezoelectric, dielectric, and pyroelectric properties, along with ionic contributions ( $ Ca^{2+} $,  $ K^{+} $,  $ Na^{+} $), generate electrical potentials in native tissues. Electroactive materials such as polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF), poly-L-lactic acid (PLLA), polypyrrole, chitosan, collagen, and cellulose, combined with small molecules, growth factors, cells, and external electrical stimulation, can synergistically enhance osteochondral repair. (Image created with BioRender; agreement number: DY28BJQ2ND.)

Figure 2. Overview of natural and synthetic electroactive materials applicable for osteochondral regeneration. Dielectric materials (e.g., zirconia, tricalcium phosphate [TCP]), piezoelectric materials (e.g., polyvinylidene fluoride [PVDF], poly-L-lactic acid [PLLA], chitosan), conductive polymers (e.g., polyaniline [PANI], polypyrrole [PPy], poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene) [PEDOT]), and conductive fillers (e.g., carbon nanotubes, nickel, graphene oxide, bioactive glass) are illustrated as promising strategies to promote osteochondral tissue repair. (Image created using BioRender; agreement number: CH28BJR99G.)

Figure 3. Comparison between a healthy knee joint and an osteoarthritic (OA) knee. In the normal knee, firm articular cartilage and an intact meniscus support smooth joint function. In contrast, the osteoarthritic knee exhibits cartilage degradation, bone spur formation, and inflammation, leading to structural alterations and impaired joint function. (Image created using BioRender; agreement number: GJ28BJRMKA.)

Figure 4. Combining strategies like electrical stimulation and conductive material loaded with cells and bone morphogenic proteins could improve bone regeneration. This includes incorporating bone morphogenic proteins with polymers like PLA, PLGA, and HA to produce the innovative biomaterial scaffold. Further, implantation of an ultrasound-stimulated scaffold promoted bone regeneration. Reproduced with permission from ref 67. Copyright 2025, Elsevier.

Figure 5. Damaged cartilage was removed, and a hydrogel loaded with electrically stimulated chondrocytes was surgically implanted in defective articular cartilage to promote regeneration. Reproduced with permission from ref 9. Available under a CC-BY-4.0. Copyright 2019, MDPI, Farooqi et al.

Figure 6. (a) This image shows a rabbit femur defect treated with piezoelectric injectable hydrogel with and without ultrasound stimulation for 1–2 months. (b) represents  $ \mu $-CT images of the defect. (c) ICRS histological criteria score macroscopic evaluation of cartilage for 2 months. (d) represents the volume of subchondral bone formed inside the defect. These results validate the potential of PLLA-based injectable hydrogel for enhanced cartilage healing in vivo. Reproduced with permission from ref 83. Available under a CC-BY-4.0. Copyright 2023, Vinikoor et al.

anchors.text:
Figure 1.
A 3D reconstruction of a left scapula (posterolateral view). The scapular plane was defined by 3 points at the center of the glenoid (C), the inferior scapular angle (IS) and the point at the vertebral border where the scapular spine intersects the medial border of the scapula (MS). A Cartesian coordinate system was defined with the origin at point C, with the x-axis normal to the scapular plane, the z-axis connecting MS and C, and the y-axis defined by the cross product of × and z axes. Glenoid height was measured as the distance between the most superior (S) and most inferior (I) points of the glenoid rim, glenoid width as the distance between the most anterior (A) and most posterior (P) points of the glenoid rim. The glenoid version (α) was measured as the angle subtended by a line connecting points A and P and the x-axis.

Figure 2.
Examples of DRRs showing the CSA measurement which is the angle subtended by a line connecting the superior and inferior border of the glenoid fossa and another connecting the inferior border of the glenoid with the most infero-lateral point of the acromion in true AP views (left panes). Incremental increases in anteversion (upper row) and extension (lower row) are also shown. The viewing perspective altered the visualization of the most inferolateral reference point of the acromion and consequently the CSA. Note the changing relationship between the infero-lateral acromion and tip of the coracoid process.

Figure 3.
Suter/Henninger (SH) scapular classification system to assess the viewing perspective of an AP DRR of the scapula: the glenoid rim is marked by the yellow line. (A-D) Determination of a glenoid rim double contour. (A) Type A: none. (B) Type B: inverted teardrop double contour initiated at the upper glenoid, <50% of glenoid height. (C) Type C: teardrop double contour initiated at the lower glenoid, <50% of glenoid height. (D) Type D: double contour >50% of glenoid height. (E-G) Assessment of coracoglenoid overlap and projection of the coracoid process. (E) Type 1: Overlap of the upper glenoid rim and the coracoid process, or its inferior edge aligned with the upper glenoid rim. (F) Type 2: no overlap of the upper glenoid rim and the coracoid process, coracoid process is above the upper glenoid rim. (G) Type 3: no overlap of the upper glenoid rim and the coracoid process, coracoid process is below the upper glenoid rim or its superior edge aligned with the upper glenoid rim.

Figure 4.
CSA measured for 10 scapulae in extension/flexion (top) and anteversion/retroversion (middle) viewing perspectives. The grey lines indicate the normal range of CSA from Moor et al. $ ^{30} $ The standard deviation of CSA typically increased as the viewing perspective increased, with more CSA values outside the normal threshold. There were significant differences in CSA between non-AP and true AP views. In flexion/extension the CSA increased with viewing angle. In anteversion the CSA increased with viewing angle, whereas the CSA decreased with increased retroversion. The difference between the non-AP and true AP CSA at different viewing perspectives (bottom). The CSA was relatively insensitive to flexion/extension (black bars), where only  $ 30^{\circ} $ viewing angles had mean differences outside the  $ \pm2^{\circ} $ window. Beyond a  $ 5^{\circ} $ viewing angle versus true AP, anteversion and retroversion (shaded bars) resulted in more than  $ 2^{\circ} $ alteration of the CSA compared to the true AP view.

Figure 5.
Results of the linear mixed-effects model showing the “safe zone” (green) where scapula malposition may result in a CSA within  $ 2^{\circ} $ of the true AP view. 3D reconstructions of scapulae are shown to indicate the representative viewing perspective in each quadrant of the graph.

Figure 6.

anchors.text: Figure 1. Alluvial diagram illustrating the diverse effects of electrical stimulus parameters on cellular responses in cartilage tissue engineering applications. The diagram visualizes the relationship among the coupling method, electric field strength, frequency, and observed cellular behavior across 16 studies. Studies utilizing 3D bioscaffolds are denoted by an open star, highlighting their role in specific coupling conditions. The diagram emphasizes the variability in electrical stimulus protocols and their impact on cellular processes, including proliferation, differentiation, condensation, ECM synthesis, and cell viability. $ ^{26,27,29-36,93-95} $

Figure 2. Synthesis and characterization of GF. (a) Schematic illustrating the synthesis of CVD GF on a nickel (Ni) foam template. Graphene/nickel foam (Gr/Nickel) is coated with poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA) to maintain integrity during Ni etching in 3 M HCl. After Ni removal, PMMA is dissolved in an acetone bath, resulting in free-standing GF. (b) Macroscale images of Ni foam before and after graphene synthesis, and the subsequent GF bioscaffolds. (c) Cross-sectional SEM analysis revealing (i) hourglass and (ii) triangle node junctions where structure thickness is measured, and surface SEM images show the (iii) hierarchical porous structure and (iv) wrinkled surface topography of the CVD GF. (d) Raman spectra from six different GF samples, displaying the characteristic G-peak ( $ I_{G} $ at  $ \approx 1580 $ cm $ ^{-1} $) and 2D peak ( $ I_{2D} $ at  $ \approx 2700 $ cm $ ^{-1} $), confirming the graphitic structure of GF. (e) Raman spatial mapping over a 10,000  $ \mu $m $ ^2 $ area, illustrating: (i) G peak intensity, (ii) 2D peak intensity, and (iii)  $ I_{2D}/I_{G} $ ratio, which demonstrate the multilayer graphitic nature of the CVD GF with multilayer regions indicated by  $ 1 < I_{2D}/I_{G} < 1.5 $. (scale bar = 20  $ \mu $m).

Figure 3. Custom-designed electrical stimulus chambers for direct electrical stimulus in vitro. (a) Three-dimensional CAD renderings of the DLP printed electrical stimulus chambers. (b) Images illustrating various components of the assembled chambers: (i) Platinum coated tungsten wires are secured in the chamber lid for graphene foam connection, (ii) extension of wires beyond the lid for oscilloscope and function generator connection, and (iii) size comparison of the chamber on a glass slide with graphene foam in the center. (c) Wiring diagram depicting the setup for waveform monitoring across the graphene foam, including a reference resistor of 5.1 ohms for voltage verification using an oscilloscope and digital multimeter (DMM). (d) Schematic representation detailing the chamber connections, including the placement of (a) wires, (b) voltage supply, (c) oscilloscope, and (d) graphene foam. Also shown is a digital image of the connections within the fully assembled device. (e) Oscilloscope voltage readings across the graphene foam with applied biphasic square voltage inputs of 20, 40, and 60 mVpp, with an average measured RMS voltage for each input of 8.08, 16.04, and 26.71 mV, respectively.

Figure 4. Comparative cellular architecture of GF in ESCs and CCs. (a) Cellular imaging on graphene foam: (i) bright-field microscopy reveals the scaffold's structure, (ii) Hoechst 33342 staining (blue) highlights nuclei distribution, and (iii) an overlay of (i) and (ii) illustrates nuclei alignment with the scaffold. (b) Confocal microscopy showcasing cellular interaction with the scaffold: (i) nuclei (Hoechst 33342), (ii) actin fibers labeled with AF488 + 10 nm colloidal gold, (iii) an overlay of i and ii and (iv) color-coded z-stack projection depicts limitations of confocal imaging in 3D opaque GF. (c–n) MicroCT imaging contrasts cellular morphology and distribution when cultured in CC versus ESC (without electrical stimulation) displays enhanced cellular structure, density, and migration within GF: (c–f) side and zoomed views of GF-cells cultured in CC with 0% (c, e) and 60% (d, f) GF opacity show limited cellular elongation and density, (g–j) side and zoomed-in views of GF-cells cultured in ESCs display enhanced cellular elongation and density. (k–n) Top and side views of microCT in 3D: CC (k, m) show rounded, sparsely distributed cells, whereas cells in ESC (l, n) exhibit denser, more elongated cells penetrating deeply into the scaffold, aligning with graphene foam structures.

Figure 5. Mechanical characterization of GF-cell composites post ES. Bar plots illustrating the results of dynamic mechanical analysis following 14 days of cell culture with 7 days of direct electrical stimulation applied to ATDCS cells cultured on GF. (a) Stress–strain phase shift, (b) stress relaxation, (c) compressive modulus, (d) equilibrium modulus, and (e) dynamic modulus, each incorporating data points and standard deviations to reflect variability. (f) Stress–strain curves used to derive compressive modulus values, demonstrating the mechanical responses of GF-cell composites across different electrical stimulation conditions.

Figure 6. Structural dynamics and cellular interactions in GF-cell constructs. (a) Box plots illustrating the significant changes in thickness before (GF bioscaffolds) and after (GF-cell composites) cell culture. (b) SEM image depicting cells bridging structural branch cracks within GF. (c) Comparative stress–strain hysteresis loops for the initial (i) and eighth (ii) compression cycles from electrically stimulated samples, supplemented with insets that contrast the mechanical behaviors of cells cultured in control chambers and bare GF. (d) Box plots representing energy dissipation across initial and final cycles for ES samples, samples from control chambers, and bare GF. (e) Energy dissipation over compression cycle time after the first compression (t = 2) fit with an exponential decay model. (f) Adjusted energy dissipation  $ \left(y_{\text{adjusted}} = \frac{y_{\text{fit}} - y_0}{A}\right) $ plotted on a log scale to visualize changes in slopes across samples, inset with a table of the  $ y_0 $ and  $ \tau $ values.

Figure 7. Estimated cell count and representative nuclei staining for each ES condition. (a) Bar graph showing estimated cell count (# of cells/mm³) within GF samples subjected to different ES conditions: 0, 20, 40, and 60 mV. One-way ANOVA indicates a statistically significant effect of ES on cell proliferation (n = 3, F = 10.94, p = 0.0033). Tukey's post hoc comparisons reveal significant differences between specific conditions, particularly between 0 mV and both 20 and 40 mV conditions, as well as between 60 and 40 mV conditions. Representative nuclei Hoechst counterstaining images for each condition: (b) 0 mV, (c) 20, (d) 40, and (e) 60 mV ((b–e): scale bar = 300 μm).

anchors.text: Fig. 1. Serial follow-up magnetic resonance imagings (MRIs). (A) Initial preoperative MRI, T2-weighted coronal and sagittal images. A full-thickness tear of the supraspinatus tendon was observed with a medio-lateral retraction diameter of 2 cm. (B) Postoperative 6-month follow-up MRI shows an approximately  $ 18\times16\times14 $ mm peri-anchor cyst at the medial anchor within the humeral head. (C) A follow-up MRI at 1 year after surgery shows an increase in the size of the cystic lesion ( $ 25\times18\times18 $ mm) compared to the postoperative 6-month follow-up MRI. However, the continuity of the repaired cuff was well-maintained. (D) A follow-up MRI at 20 months after surgery shows extensive enlargement of the cyst ( $ 37\times22\times22 $ mm) and a change in the inclination of the medial anchor. A sagittal image shows substantial subacromial and subdeltoid effusion. (E) A follow-up MRI at 3 years post-surgery shows granulation tissue filling the cavity and apparently fused with the anchor. The integrity of the repaired rotator cuff was well-maintained. The subacromial effusion was reduced, and the size of the peri-anchor cyst had decreased slightly ( $ 35\times23\times18 $ mm). (F) A follow-up MRI at 4 years post-surgery shows decreased size of the peri-anchor cyst lesion ( $ 30\times20\times15 $ mm). Granulation tissue was fused to the anchor and filled the cavity. The continuity of the repaired tendon was well-maintained.

Fig. 2. Serial follow-up X-rays. The arrows indicate the cyst. The left-right arrows indicate the diameter of the cyst. (A) No bone abnormalities were noted on the preoperative X-ray. (B) A postoperative 3-month follow-up X-ray. An approximately  $ 5 \times 5 $ mm cyst was observed at the medial anchor site on the humeral head. (C) A postoperative 6-month follow-up X-ray. The size of cyst was slightly increased to  $ 7 \times 7 $ mm. (D) A postoperative 20-month follow-up X-ray. The size of cyst was significantly increased. Postoperative 3-year (E) and 4-year (F) X-rays show regression of the peri-anchor cyst.
Fig. 4. An ultrasonographic image at 20 months after surgery. Aspiration of subacromial effusion and corticosteroid injection were performed under sonographic guidance.

Fig. 3. Intraoperative arthroscopic findings. (A) A 5.0-mm Paladin anchor (Bioabsorbable; CONMED, Utica, NY, USA) was used for medial row fixation. Rotator cuff repair was performed using the transosseous equivalent repair technique. (B) View from the additional arthroscopy performed at 4 years and 2 months after the primary surgery. Arthroscopy shows that the continuity of the repaired cuff is well-maintained.

A$_{2A}$ (E, F) and A$_{3}$AR (G, H) expression on hFOB 1.19 osteoblasts in control condition (E, G) and after 24 hours exposure to PEMFs (F, H). Original magnification 400×.

Effect of A₂₄AR agonist and antagonist (CGS 21680, 100 nM; SCH 442416, 1 µM) or A₃AR agonist and antagonist (CI-IB-MECA, 100 nM; MRS 1334, 1 µM) on cell proliferation in the absence or in the presence of PEMF exposure for 24 hours in T/C-28a2 chondrocytes (C) and in hFOB 1.19 osteoblasts (D). anchors.text: Fig. 1 | Structural changes of tendons in tendinopathy. Normal tendon is a well-organized network of collagen fibrils. The extracellular matrix (ECM) is dense, with a fibrillary network of predominantly parallel-aligned collagen fibres, principally consisting of type I collagen. The ECM is composed of proteoglycans, glycosaminoglycans and glycoproteins including small leucine-rich proteoglycans. In tendinopathy, tenocytes are decreased in volume, becoming longer and slender, have an increased nucleus to cytoplasm ratio and produce less ECM but with an increase in type III collagen density (mostly owing to less degradation). Histological examination of patient biopsy sample has shown intratendinous collagen degeneration with fibre disorientation and glycosaminoglycan accumulation between the thinning fibrils with inflammatory cell infiltrates. Neovascularization and neoinervation are also frequently found in the diseased tendon.

Fig. 2 | Common sites of tendinopathy. This figure shows the incidence of different types of tendinopathy in the general population. Most tendinopathies in the lower limbs involve the Achilles tendons or patellar tendons, although current studies have highlighted the growing incidence of gluteal tendinopathy. The most frequent tendinopathy in the upper limbs affects the rotator cuff tendons and the elbow (extensor carpi radialis brevis), commonly known as tennis elbow or lateral elbow tendinopathy.

Fig. 3 | Pathophysiology of tendinopathy. Various risk factors including excess mechanical overuse as well as environmental factors including smoking, metabolic diseases (for example, diabetes mellitus and hyperlipidaemia) and certain medications (for example, fluoroquinolones and excessive use of corticosteroids) can trigger the development of tendinopathy. The concept of preclinical disease, in which clinical symptoms are not apparent, is supported by genetic susceptibility datasets. Studies have identified single-nucleotide variants in COL5A1, MMP3, TIMP2 and TNC. Human tissue studies analysing asymptomatic tendons show dysregulation of extracellular matrix, immune responses and stromal responses. Failure of normal homeostatic responses eventually leads to early tendinopathy with influx of immune cells, stromal cell dysfunction, apoptosis, oxidative stress and matrix dysfunction. Dysregulation of repair mechanisms (such as auto-amplificatory loops and matrix-stromal-immune crosstalk dysfunction) leads to established or chronic tendinopathy with the clinical features of poor function, pain and load capacity.

Fig. 4 | Molecular mechanisms of tendinopathy. Molecular mechanisms of tendinopathy encompass four distinct compartments. The stromal compartment includes tissue-resident tenocytes and matrix components (such as collagen, extracellular matrix (ECM) proteins, interfascicular matrix and small leucine-rich proteoglycans), which are essential for tissue remodelling and repair. In diseased states, tendons acquire a stromal ‘signature’ with altered surface markers (podoplanin, VCAM1 and endosialin) and perturbed intracellular signal pathways that have functional consequences (such as matrix regulation, immune cell recruitment and cell proliferation) relevant to tendon pathology. For example, activation of the MAPK pathway by IL-33, IL-6 and IL-17 or the NF- $ \kappa $B pathway by TNF or 15-epi-lipoxin A, or the JAK-STAT pathway by IL-13 and IL-4 result in downstream modulation of enhanced cytokine and chemokine production, ECM remodelling, proliferation and angiogenesis, all of which become dysregulated in tendon disease. The immune compartment involving T cells, dendritic cells, mast cells and macrophages (pro-inflammatory versus pro-resolving) respond to initial tissue insult through damage-associated molecular patterns or pathogen-associated molecular patterns. Immune cell recruitment, which in normal circumstances represents a homeostatic inflammatory response, becomes aberrant in tendon disease. The neural compartment, which in the homeostatic state plays a role in proprioception, interacts with mast cells to modulate adaptive responses in the normal tendon. However, in tendinopathy, excessive stimulation leads to tissue breakdown, degeneration and neoinervation involving the glutamatergic and autonomic systems. The release of neuropeptides, such as substance P and calcitonin gene-related peptide, stimulates mast cell degranulation, releasing a variety of agents, which modulate a variety of cellular activities in the matrix. Although most tendons are poorly vascularized, they respond to hypoxia by secreting angiogenic factors (VEGF or HIF1 $ \alpha $) that induce the growth of neovessels, which comprise the vascular compartment of tendinopathy pathogenesis. Fibrin-rich exudates leak from the neovascular, resulting in fibrinoid degeneration, a typical feature of structural alterations in tendinopathy. The complex molecular interactions among these four compartments comprise a critical balance between tissue repair and return to homeostasis versus further degeneration within the tendon. HSPs, heat shock proteins.

Fig. 5 | Management of tendinopathy. Early diagnosis is key and should consider a thorough differential diagnosis and the International Consensus (ICON) 2019 consensus guidelines $ ^{107} $. A patient-centred and personalized approach should be considered in every case. Education on the disease process along with acknowledgement of previous unsuccessful treatments (if appropriate) and potential prolonged time frames involved in management as well as appreciation of fear mechanisms involved with commencing treatment should be undertaken. First-line treatment should encompass an individualized tailored loading programme, referred to as the precision tendinopathy management plan. This approach may include isotonic, isometric, eccentric, energy storage loading versus energy storage and release. Importantly, patient engagement and re-evaluation within a 3-month period is crucial to determine loading progression and consideration of adjunct therapies in combination with education and psychosocial factors. Throughout the ensuing months, revisiting this cycle may be required with further changes in loading programmes or adjunct therapies. Surgical intervention may be considered in the recalcitrant non-responders after 12 months of a personalized loading programme. ESWT, extracorporeal shockwave therapy; GTN, glyceryl trinitrate.

anchors.text: Figure 1. Experimental test setup. (a) The processed 6 well tissue culture plate with titanium electrodes. (b) Technical drawing of the system for capacitively coupled electric field stimulation.

Figure 2. Numerical simulation of electric fields within the experimental test setup. (a) The electric field distribution simulated with COMSOL Multiphysics®, v5.3a at the bottom of the Petri dish and (b) at 1 mm above the bottom for a potential difference of 1 V. At an amplitude of 141.4 mV, the result has to be scaled by a factor of 0.1414, yielding e.g., a maximum field of about 5.7 µV/m instead of 40 µV/m at 1 V amplitude.
Figure 3. Scheme of the experimental procedure.

Figure 4. Cellular activity of human chondrocytes following electrical stimulation with 1 kHz and either 100 mV or 1 V. Chondrocytes derived from non-degenerative (n = 4) or osteoarthritic (OA) cartilage (n = 6) were seeded on collagen scaffolds and stimulated over a period of seven days. Afterwards, metabolic activity was determined via water-soluble tetrazolium salt (WST-1) assay (a) and DNA content was analyzed by peqGOLD Tissue DNA Mini Kit (b). Data are presented as boxplots. Statistical analysis within a stimulation group was performed with Friedman test (# p < 0.05). To compare two samples between OA and non-degenerative chondrocytes, Mann-Whitney-U-test was performed (* p < 0.05, ** p < 0.01).

Figure 5. Relative gene expression of chondrogenic differentiation markers in human chondrocytes after electrical stimulation with 100 mV and 1 V at 1 kHz. Chondrocytes derived from non-degenerative (n = 4) or osteoarthritic (OA) cartilage (n = 6) were seeded on collagen scaffolds and electrical stimulation was performed over a period of seven days. Afterwards, RNA was isolated to determine the gene expression of chondrogenic differentiation markers via semi-quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR). Data are presented as boxplots of the percentage of  $ 2^{(-\Delta\Delta Ct)} $ related to unstimulated cells (100%). Statistical analysis within a stimulation group was performed with Friedman test by using the  $ \Delta\Delta Ct $-values (\# p < 0.05).

Figure 6. Release of collagen (Col) II and glycosaminoglycans (GAG) in human chondrocytes after electrical stimulation with 100 mV and 1 V at 1 kHz. Chondrocytes derived from non-degenerative (n = 4) or osteoarthritic (OA) cartilage (n = 6) were seeded on collagen scaffolds and stimulated over a period of 7 days. Afterwards, protein synthesis rates of Col II were determined using ELISA. Glycosaminoglycans (GAG) were analyzed by Blyscan Sulfated Glycosaminoglycan Assay™. Data are presented as boxplots. Statistical analysis within a stimulation group was performed with Friedman test (# p < 0.05, ## p < 0.01). To compare two samples between OA and non-degenerative chondrocytes Mann-Whitney-U-test was performed (* p < 0.05, ** p < 0.01).

Figure 7. Relative gene expression rates of de-differentiation and hypertrophy markers in chondrocytes after electrical stimulation with 100 mV and 1 V at 1 kHz. Chondrocytes derived from non-degenerative (n = 4) or osteoarthritic (OA) cartilage (n = 6) were seeded on collagen scaffolds and stimulated over a period of seven days. Afterwards, the gene expression of chondrogenic de-differentiation and hypertrophy markers was determined via a semi-quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR). Data are presented as boxplots of the percentage of 2 $ (-\Delta C t) $ related to unstimulated cells (100%). Statistical analysis within a stimulation group was performed with Friedman test by using the  $ \Delta C t $-values (\# p < 0.05).

Figure 8. Collagen I release of human chondrocytes after electrical stimulation with 100 mV and 1 V at 1 kHz. Chondrocytes derived from non-degenerative (n = 4) or osteoarthritic (OA) cartilage (n = 6) were seeded on collagen scaffolds and stimulated over a period of seven days. Afterwards, protein biosynthesis of collagen I was detected in supernatants using the MicroVue CICP assay. Data are presented as boxplots. Statistical analysis within a stimulation group was performed with the Friedman test ( $ \#\# p < 0.01 $). To compare two samples between OA and non-degenerative chondrocytes Mann-Whitney-U-test was performed ( $ ^{**} p < 0.01 $).

anchors.text: Fig. 1 Illustration shows the highly vascularized ECM of bone (Bone ECM) and avascular ECM of cartilage (cartilage ECM)

Fig. 2 Schematic diagram of ca $ ^{2+} $ signal transduction pathway and other miscellaneous pathways activate in response to the electrical and mechanical stimulations. The mechanical stimulation on piezoelectric scaffold will result in the electrical signal generation and which will stimulate the voltage-gated ca $ ^{2+} $ channel. Further increase in the intracellular Ca $ ^{2+} $ concentration activates the calmodulin (an abbreviation of the calcium-modulated protein) and which will further activate the calcineurin (calcium and calmodulin-dependent serine/threonine protein phosphatase). The activated calcineurin dephosphorylates the NF-AT and it will translocate to the nucleus, where it acts in conjunction with other associated proteins as transcription factors. Also the mechanical stimulation itself can activate the mechanoreceptors present in the membrane and which will lead to the activation of PKC and MAPK signaling cascades. These cascades will result in the synthesis of proteoglycan and inhibition of IL-1, responsible for the breakdown of proteoglycan

FIGURE 1.

(A) Optimization of rabbit articular chondrocyte harvest. Articular cartilage tissues were retrieved from skeletally mature New Zealand White Rabbits and subjected to collagenase I digestion using various concentrations (0.1, 1.0, 2.5, 5.0 mg/ml) for 5 hours. Recovered articular cartilage cells were cultured in complete DMEM/F12 medium supplemented with 20% fetal calf serum. Cultured chondrocytes under different digestion conditions were shown at three days after isolation. (B) Isolation and culture of rabbit articular chondrocytes. After optimization, articular chondrocytes were isolated using 1.0 mg/ml of collagenase for 5 hours. Morphology of the cultured cells was examined under a bright field microscope at 2, 5, 7, and 10 days after plating. Magnification, 200x.

FIGURE 2.
(A) Recombinant adenovirus-mediated efficient gene transfer into primary articular chondrocytes. Cultured articular chondrocytes were seeded in 24-well cell culture plates and infected with an adenoviral vector expressing green fluorescent protein (i.e., AdGFP) at a pre-optimized titer (multiplicity of infection, or MOI = 50). Expression of GFP was examined at 24, 48, and 72 hours after infection using fluorescence microscopy. (B) Histogram displaying the Total Image Value (TIV) of fluorescence. The total amount of fluorescence was calculated with NIH ImageJ software to quantify the amount of GFP expression. See text for more details.

FIGURE 3.

(A) Survival and gene expression of primary articular chondrocytes seeded in four different scaffold carriers. Subconfluent articular chondrocytes were infected with AdGFP at the MOI = 50. At 24 hours after infection, cells were collected by trypsinization and suspended in complete DMEM/F12 medium. Approximately 50 μl cells (approx.  $ 2 \times 10^6 $ cells per seeding) were mixed with hyaluronic acid (HA) or fibrin glue, or added to type I collagen sponge or OPLA carriers. The cell-containing carriers were placed in 48-well cell culture plates, which were kept in a well-moistened CO₂ incubator. Expression of GFP was examined at 2, 5, and 10 days after cell seeding with fluorescence microscopy. Representative results from three independent experiments are shown. (B) Histogram comparing Total Image Value (TIV) of the different carriers at different time points. The TIV was calculated with the NIH ImageJ software for each time point for each carrier and the results are displayed in the histogram.

FIGURE 4.
Quantitative assessment of transgene expression of primary articular chondrocytes seeded in four different scaffold carriers. Subconfluent rabbit articular chondrocytes were infected with AdGL3-Luc at the MOI = 50. At 24 hours after infection, cells were collected by trypsinization and suspended in complete DMEM/F12 medium. Approximately 50 μl cells (approx.  $ 2 \times 10^6 $ cells per seeding) were mixed with hyaluronic acid (HA) or fibrin glue, or added to type I collagen sponge or OPLA carriers. The cell-containing carriers were placed in 48-well cell culture plates, which were kept in a well-moistened CO₂ incubator. Luciferase activity was assayed at 24 and 48 hours after cell seeding. Each assay conditions were done in duplicate. ANOVA analysis was conducted on the quantitative data (see text for detail). Representative results from two independent batches of experiments are shown.

FIGURE 5.
Matrix production of articular chondrocytes seeded in the OPLA scaffold carrier. Primary articular chondrocytes were seeded into OPLA plugs (approximately  $ 2 \times 10^{6} $ cells per seeding). Controls (OPLA Only) were done with medium only. At four weeks after plating, OPLA carriers were fixed with 1.0% glutaraldehyde. The fixed OPLA carriers were embedded in OCT medium and frozen sectioned (a to d), with some sections stained with Alcian blue (b and d). Alternatively, the fixed OPLA carriers were first subjected to Alcian blue staining, and then frozen sectioning (e). The fixed OPLA carriers were also stained with hematoxylin-eosin (f). Each condition was performed in triplicate. Representative results from two independent experiments are shown.

anchors.text: Figure 1. Visual representation of this research includes preprinting, printing, and postprinting stages. Preprinting stage: synthesis of Ti₃C₂Tₓ MXene and GGO. SEM, Raman, and XRD characterization confirmed the processing and layer information. A plate-plate rheometer flow sweep was used to observe the shear thinning behavior and shear stress response, and filament string and collapse tests were performed to validate the printability of the inks. Printing stage: printing parameters determined from the previous stage were employed using CELLINK's BIO X printer to print scaffold structures. Postprinting stage: scaffolds were tested in compression to failure or load cell limit to quantify mechanical qualities such as stiffness (Young's modulus). A 4-point method was used, where inks were printed across four silver contacts with the supplied current delivered at 100 μA, and the voltage drop across the inner two contacts was measured. The change in voltage and current was used with Ohm's law to determine a value for conductivity. Mouse myoblasts were mixed into the inks, printed, cultured for 48 h, and then assayed to demonstrate biocompatibility. Figure made with biorender.com.

Figure 2. NM characterization of bulk material: (A–C) GGO and (D–F) Ti_{3}C_{2}T_{x} (A, D) Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images highlight the layered morphology characteristic of the production processes associated with each material. (B, E) Raman spectra were all collected at a wavelength of 532 nm. (C, F) X-ray diffraction (XRD) pattern demonstrating relative chemical composition.

Figure 3. Rheological characterization of bioinks. (A–C) Shear-dependent viscosity and (D–F) shear stress responses measured using a parallel-plate rheometer at 25 °C. (A, D) Comparison of CELLINK, GGO (2 mg/mL), and Ti₃C₂Tₓ (2 mg/mL) formulations showing characteristic shear-thinning behavior. (B, E) Concentration-dependent rheological response of Ti₃C₂Tₓ bioinks (0–8 mg/mL). (C, F) Concentration-dependent rheological response of GGO bioinks (0–8 mg/mL). All inks exhibited non-Newtonian, shear-thinning behavior with viscosity decreasing as shear rate increased. All inks demonstrate an acceptable window of shear rates.⁹⁰

Figure 4. Printability characterization of inks: (A, B) CELLINK, (C, D) GGO, and (E, F) Ti₃C₂Tₓ (A, C, E) A filament string test was performed to validate the printability of the inks and hone the correct print pressure. (B, D, F) Filament collapse test was performed, ink was printed across a structure with gaps of 1, 2, 4, 8, and 16 mm to show stability and optimize print speed.

Figure 5. Mechanical and electrical testing results of CELLINK, Ti₃C₂Tₓ and GGO prepared scaffolds. Measurements were taken at 25 °C. (A) Compression stress—strain curve. Scaffolds were tested in compression to failure or load cell limit to quantify compressive Young’s modulus (ANOVA, post hoc analysis,  $ ^8 = P < 0.05 $). The shaded regions on stress—strain curves represent  $ \pm 1 $ standard deviation ( $ n = 3 $). (B) Electrical conductivity of printed CELLINK, GGO, and Ti₃C₂Tₓ bioinks measured using a four-point probe configuration at a fixed current of 100  $ \mu $A. Conductivity was calculated from the measured resistance. Bars represent mean  $ \pm $ standard deviation ( $ n = 3 $). The calculated conductivities were  $ 0.46 \pm 0.03 $ S/m for CELLINK,  $ 0.58 \pm 0.14 $ S/m for GGO, and  $ 0.97 \pm 0.08 $ S/m for Ti₃C₂Tₓ bioinks. The Ti₃C₂Tₓ formulation showed significantly higher conductivity compared to CELLINK and GGO (ANOVA with post hoc analysis,  $ ^8 = P < 0.05 $). Inset: qualitative LED test demonstrating brighter illumination through the Ti₃C₂Tₓ hydrogel, consistent with its higher conductivity.

Figure 6. Cell viability and bioink imaging. (A, B, C) Live dead imaging, Mouse myoblasts were mixed into the inks, printed and cultured for 48 h then stained and imaged green = live, red = dead. (D) Percent of live cells as a ratio of live cells to total cells to quantify the biocompatibility of the inks, there is no significant difference across groups (P < 0.5). (E, F, G) transmitted light imaging demonstrates particle size and distribution. (A, E) CELLINK. (B, F) GGO. (C, G) Ti₃C₂Tₓ. All scale bars are 200 μm. (H) LDH release measured at 48 h shows cytotoxicity levels for 2D plated cells, CELLINK, GGO (2 mg/mL), and Ti₃C₂Tₓ (2 mg/mL); values are expressed as percent LDH activity normalized to maximal release. There is no significant difference across groups (P < 0.5).

Figure 7. String test assessing the printability of bioinks using three nozzle sizes. Representative images show extrusion behavior for 22 gauge (top row, blue), 25 gauge (middle row, red), and 27 gauge (bottom row, clear) conical nozzles across all ink formulations and concentrations (0.5–8 mg/mL). The test was used to determine the minimum pressure required for continuous, uniform filament formation without breakage or spreading.

Figure 8. Conductivity (S/m) and compression modulus (kPa) of Cartilage, $ ^{109-111} $ Neurons, $ ^{109,112} $ Skeletal, $ ^{109,113,114} $ and Cardiac Muscle $ ^{113,114} $ compared to  $ * $ = the inks in this study CELLINK, GGO, and Ti $ _3 $C $ _2 $T $ _x $ bioink. Icons from biorender.com.

(b) The deposited calcium was normalized against the surface cell number, which was determined using a LDH assay. anchors.text: Measurements on anteroposterior and axillary radiographs. The true anteroposterior radiograph of the shoulder (Fig. 1-A) depicts the measurement of HGA-SI by drawing a best-fit circle on the humeral head with a line originating from the center of the circle parallel to the glenoid center peg. The HGA-SI was determined as the difference between the line and the center peg of the glenoid (arrow). The axillary view of the shoulder (Fig. 1-B) depicts measurement of glenoid retroversion by drawing a line parallel to the body of the scapula, similar to that used with the technique described by Friedman et al.²⁶ for CT measurement, and a line (the glenoid axis [dashed line]) overlapping the center peg of the glenoid (arrow). The angle between these two lines (*) represents the amount of version of the glenoid.

Grading system for the Anchor Peg Glenoid implant. Grade 1 (Fig. 2-A) indicates marked osteolysis around the center peg (inset) of the glenoid component as identified by the radiopaque marker. Grade 2 (Fig. 2-B) is defined as bone integration to the edges of the flanges of the center peg (inset), but not within it. Grade 3 (Fig. 2-C) is defined as bone integration within the flanges of the center peg (inset).
